title: Like an infant
hook: can you soften your breath like a baby's? give birth without possessing (Tao Te Ching 10)

segments.voice: Yesterday's word and line were the same: stop before it spills, and step back when the work is done.

A baby asleep on a parent's chest. Watch the belly, not the face. It rises, it falls, and nothing else in the body seems to be helping or fighting. No clenched jaw. No shoulders up near the ears. Now check your own breath, right where it is, without fixing it. Is it soft, or is it working? Chapter ten of the Tao Te Ching holds up that sleeping baby as a kind of teacher, and this chapter doesn't instruct. It asks.
screen: `A BABY ASLEEP.` → `WATCH THE BELLY.` → `CHAPTER TEN ASKS.`

segments.voice: First, a string of questions. Can you hold body and spirit together, and not let them drift apart? Can you gather your breath and make it soft, like an infant's? Can you wipe your inner sight clean? Can you care for people without cleverness? The chapter doesn't answer them. They're left open, like a hard question left on the board overnight. Second, why an infant? A baby hasn't learned to brace yet, to hold its breath before a hard conversation or tighten up in traffic. The softness isn't a technique it practiced; it simply hasn't been trained out of it. The chapter seems to ask whether a grown person can find their way back to that, on purpose. Third, softness isn't weakness. Two days ago, chapter eight praised water for doing good without competing. A soft breath has the same quiet strength, small enough to carry in your own chest. Fourth, from breath to what you make. The chapter closes with a list: to give life and not possess it, to act and not lean on it, to lead and not control. The book calls this a hidden kind of virtue. A parent knows its shape: you raise a child, and the child is not yours to own. The soft breath and the open hand sit side by side in the same chapter.
screen: `A CHAPTER OF QUESTIONS.` · `A BABY HASN'T LEARNED TO BRACE.` · `SOFT ISN'T WEAK.` · `GIVE LIFE, AND DON'T POSSESS IT.` · then, large: `CAN YOU MAKE YOUR BREATH SOFT?`

segments.voice: Sit or lie down with one hand on your belly, and let the breath come in without pulling and go out without pushing. Not slow, not deep, only soft, like the sleeping baby's; if you notice bracing in the jaw, the shoulders or the hands, let that one place go. When a thought pulls you away, come back to the hand rising and falling.
Like an infant. Chapter ten's picture for a breath that isn't bracing against anything, and a life that gives without holding on. Today's word.
Your line: soft breath. Nothing to fix, only something to let go of. See you at chapter eleven.

howItsDone: Some people who read the Tao Te Ching pair chapter ten with a few minutes of quiet, unforced breathing, letting the breath move on its own instead of controlling it.

chat.says: Why would the Tao Te Ching hold up a baby as a teacher?
options: Its breath is soft and unbraced, and the chapter asks if adults can find that again.
Because babies know the Tao and can teach it to their parents in words.
Because it says adults should stop thinking and act on every impulse.
